**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware — expansion vs. utilisation
**Status:** For discussion before Thursday's planning session

We've reached the point where our inference workloads are bumping against the ceiling of our current hardware, and the obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more GPUs or squeeze more out of the eight A100s we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because I don't believe the framing "we're out of capacity, therefore we buy" is the right one, and I want to make sure we decide deliberately rather than by momentum.

The case for buying is straightforward. Our queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and the product team has flagged latency as a growing source of complaints. Every week we defer a purchase is a week we're arguably degrading the experience for our heaviest users. Hardware prices are also relatively stable right now, and lead times, while not trivial, are manageable. If demand keeps growing at anything like the current rate, we will need more silicon eventually — the only real question is when.

But the case for improving utilisation first is stronger than it might initially appear, and it rests on three things: cost, information, and reversibility.

On cost: our current fleet sits at roughly 55% average utilisation, but that number hides a lot. Nightly batch jobs, staging environments holding reservations they no longer need, and models kept resident in memory "just in case" all consume capacity that could serve production traffic. Industry experience — and our own preliminary audit — suggests that better scheduling, quantisation of two of our largest models, and aggressive batching could plausibly lift effective throughput by 30–40% without a single new purchase. Even if we only realise half of that, it defers a capital outlay of several hundred thousand dollars by two quarters or more. That money has opportunity cost: it's the same budget that would fund a second engineer, a proper observability stack, or a larger safety net for the reliability work we keep deferring.

On information: if we buy hardware now, we learn nothing except that we can spend money. If we invest a month in utilisation work first, we learn what our true demand curve looks like once the artificial constraints are removed. There's a real risk that our perceived capacity crunch is partly an artefact of inefficiency, and buying now would lock us into paying for headroom we didn't actually need. Conversely, if utilisation work stalls and demand keeps climbing, the purchase case becomes overwhelming and we'll have lost only a few weeks.

On reversibility: this is the asymmetry that matters most. A capital purchase is largely irreversible — GPUs depreciate, consume power, occupy rack space, and carry maintenance burden whether or not we need them. Utilisation improvements are cheap to attempt and, if they fail, cost us little. When one option is reversible and the other is not, and both plausibly address the problem, the reversible option should generally go first. It buys us the option to make the big decision later with better information, which is itself valuable.

On reliability, I want to be honest about a counterargument: a larger fleet gives us more redundancy, and right now a single node failure removes a meaningful fraction of our capacity. Better utilisation does nothing for that. My response is that redundancy can be addressed more cheaply through improved failover handling and workload migration than through idle spare hardware, and that a denser, better-scheduled fleet is actually easier to fail over from than a sprawl of half-idle machines.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next four to six weeks to a focused utilisation effort — scheduling, quantisation, batching, and reclaiming stale reservations — with a hard checkpoint at the end. If we've lifted effective capacity by 25% or more, we defer purchase by at least a quarter and revisit with fresh data. If we've gained less than 15%, we proceed with the purchase immediately, and I'll sponsor that request personally.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here honestly. My utilisation estimates come partly from vendor benchmarks and partly from a two-day audit; real gains could fall short. Demand forecasts are also soft, and if a new product launch lands mid-quarter, all of this arithmetic changes. That's precisely why I favour the reversible path first: it keeps us agile in the face of forecasts we shouldn't fully trust.

I'd like to hear objections before Thursday — particularly from anyone who believes the latency pain is already past the point where a six-week delay is defensible. If the product team feels that strongly, that's a legitimate input and may change the calculus. But absent that, I think the disciplined move is clear.

— Infrastructure Lead
